items.stem: An advert appears in a teen sports magazine and uses hashtags. Who is the most likely target audience?
items.answer: Teenagers who play sport
items.markingKey: Teenagers who play sport. Placement and features suggest the audience.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for running shoes, printed in a teen sports magazine.

[Image: a girl sprints up concrete steps at dawn; the city below is still asleep.]
THEY SAID TOO YOUNG. THEY SAID TOO SMALL. THEY SAID TOO LATE.
She said: watch me.
STRIDE X – featherlight foam, grip that never quits.
Your city. Your rules. Your run.
#RunYourWay  |  Available now in 12 colours.

State the main purpose of the text and explain how one feature helps to achieve it.
items.answer: To persuade young readers to buy STRIDE X by linking the shoes with determination and proving doubters wrong. Supporting evidence: "grip that never quits" (hyperbole) – the exaggeration suggests the shoes are completely reliable, like a loyal teammate.
items.markingKey: To persuade young readers to buy STRIDE X by linking the shoes with determination and proving doubters wrong. Supporting evidence: "grip that never quits" (hyperbole) – the exaggeration suggests the shoes are completely reliable, like a loyal teammate. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following persuasive letter from a student to her head teacher in Copenhagen.

Dear Ms Larsen,
I am writing on behalf of the Grade 8 class to propose a covered bike shelter for our school.
At present, 140 students cycle to school, but there are only 40 spaces. Bikes are left in the rain and two were stolen last month.
A shelter would keep bikes safe, encourage more students to cycle, and support our city's aim to be carbon-neutral by 2025.
Surely a school that teaches us about climate change should make the green choice the easy choice?
Yours sincerely,
Freja Nielsen, Grade 8B

Who is the target audience of the text? Refer to two details that suggest this audience.
items.answer: The head teacher, who has the power to approve the shelter; the formal salutation and respectful tone suit her. Supporting evidence: "Surely a school that teaches us about climate change should make the green choice the easy choice?" (rhetorical question) – it challenges the head teacher to act on the school's own values.
items.markingKey: The head teacher, who has the power to approve the shelter; the formal salutation and respectful tone suit her. Supporting evidence: "Surely a school that teaches us about climate change should make the green choice the easy choice?" (rhetorical question) – it challenges the head teacher to act on the school's own values. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Rewrite the slogan "Buy our cereal" for (a) young children and (b) health-conscious parents.
items.answer: (a) e.g. "Crunchy, munchy fun in every bowl!" (b) e.g. "Wholegrain goodness to start their day right." 1 mark each for audience-appropriate language.
items.markingKey: (a) e.g. "Crunchy, munchy fun in every bowl!" (b) e.g. "Wholegrain goodness to start their day right." 1 mark each for audience-appropriate language.

items.stem: Suggest the target audience and purpose of an advert for a new energy drink that shows skateboarders and uses slang.
items.answer: Audience: teenagers or young adults interested in extreme sports. Purpose: to persuade them to buy the drink by associating it with excitement and youth culture.
items.markingKey: Audience: teenagers or young adults interested in extreme sports. Purpose: to persuade them to buy the drink by associating it with excitement and youth culture.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Advertisers aimed at teenagers are more manipulative than those aimed at adults."
items.answer: All advertising seeks to influence; teenagers may be especially targeted through social media, so media literacy matters for every audience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: teenagers are influenced by peer pressure and social media; adverts use insecurities about image. Arguments against: adult adverts also exploit fears (health, status); many teenagers are media-literate and critical. Supported judgement: All advertising seeks to influence; teenagers may be especially targeted through social media, so media literacy matters for every audience.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "demographic".
items.answer: A group defined by characteristics such as age, gender, income or interests
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a group defined by characteristics such as age, gender, income or interests. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "Do I need it? Will I wear it 30 times?" Which technique is used?
items.answer: Rhetorical questions
items.markingKey: Rhetorical questions. The questions make readers think rather than answer aloud.

items.stem: "A rhetorical question expects the audience to answer." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A rhetorical question is asked for effect; the answer is implied, and it makes the audience think or agree.
items.markingKey: A rhetorical question is asked for effect; the answer is implied, and it makes the audience think or agree. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between emotive language and statistics.
items.answer: Emotive language persuades through feelings (pathos); statistics persuade through apparent facts and logic (logos). Strong persuasion often combines both.
items.markingKey: Emotive language persuades through feelings (pathos); statistics persuade through apparent facts and logic (logos). Strong persuasion often combines both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Write a persuasive sentence for a campaign to save a local park that uses emotive language and a statistic.
items.answer: Any sentence using both, e.g. "Over 3,000 children play in Green Park every week – will we really let bulldozers destroy their only green space?" 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: Any sentence using both, e.g. "Over 3,000 children play in Green Park every week – will we really let bulldozers destroy their only green space?" 1 mark each.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student council president to her school assembly in Toronto.

Good morning, everyone. Raise your hand if you checked your phone before breakfast today. (Pause.) Me too.
We are the most connected generation in history – and, according to our own school survey, 62 per cent of us say we feel lonely every week. Connected, but alone.
I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake. I'm asking for one hour. One lunchtime a week, phones in our bags, eyes on each other.
Let's try it. Let's talk. Let's remember what our friends' faces look like when they laugh.

Explain how the movement from a personal hook to evidence to a call to action contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: The movement from a personal hook to evidence to a call to action: it gains attention, proves the problem and then gives the audience something specific to do.
items.markingKey: The movement from a personal hook to evidence to a call to action: it gains attention, proves the problem and then gives the audience something specific to do. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a robot pet, posted on a technology website.

[Image: a silver robot puppy curled on the lap of a smiling elderly man; sunlight through a window.]
MEET PIXEL. HE NEVER NEEDS A WALK. HE NEVER FORGETS YOUR BIRTHDAY.
Powered by AI, Pixel learns your routines, reminds you of medicines and plays your favourite songs.
"I talk to him every morning," says Harold, 81, from Leeds.
Companionship, reinvented. Order today – free delivery.

Identify the technique used in ""I talk to him every morning," says Harold, 81" and explain its effect.
items.answer: Testimonial: ""I talk to him every morning," says Harold, 81" – a real-sounding customer makes the product trustworthy and emotional.
items.markingKey: Testimonial: ""I talk to him every morning," says Harold, 81" – a real-sounding customer makes the product trustworthy and emotional. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Emotive language is more persuasive than facts."
items.answer: The most persuasive texts combine emotion with evidence; emotion motivates, facts make the action seem justified.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: feelings drive action; charity adverts rely on pathos. Arguments against: facts build trust and credibility; too much emotion can feel manipulative. Supported judgement: The most persuasive texts combine emotion with evidence; emotion motivates, facts make the action seem justified.

items.stem: Choose a persuasive text you have seen. Analyse how it uses three persuasive techniques and evaluate which is most effective.
items.answer: Indicative content: three techniques with quotations; explanation of effect on the audience; reasoned judgement. Criteria A and B.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: three techniques with quotations; explanation of effect on the audience; reasoned judgement. Criteria A and B.

items.stem:
Read the following persuasive letter from a student to her head teacher in Copenhagen.

Dear Ms Larsen,
I am writing on behalf of the Grade 8 class to propose a covered bike shelter for our school.
At present, 140 students cycle to school, but there are only 40 spaces. Bikes are left in the rain and two were stolen last month.

Surely a school that teaches us about climate change should make the green choice the easy choice?

How does Freja make her letter persuasive?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: Freja opens with a clear purpose and speaks "on behalf of the Grade 8 class", giving her authority. items.stem: In a video advert, why might the director use a close-up of a child's face?
options: To show the whole landscape
To hide the child's feelings
To create an emotional connection with the viewer
To make the advert shorter
items.answer: To create an emotional connection with the viewer
items.markingKey: C. Close-ups reveal emotion.

items.stem: "Colours in adverts are chosen randomly." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Advertisers choose colours deliberately for their connotations (green for nature, red for urgency or passion, gold for luxury).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a print advertisement and a video advertisement.
items.answer: A print advert relies on a single image, layout and text that readers can study; a video advert uses moving images, camera shots, sound, music and time to tell a mini-story.
items.markingKey: A print advert relies on a single image, layout and text that readers can study; a video advert uses moving images, camera shots, sound, music and time to tell a mini-story. items.stem:
Read the following storyboard description of a 30-second charity video advertisement.

SHOT 1 (close-up): A girl's feet in torn sandals walk along a dry riverbed. Sound: wind, no music.
SHOT 2 (wide shot): She carries a yellow jerrycan towards a distant well. Caption: "Amina walks 6 km for water. Every day."
SHOT 3 (close-up): Water pours from a new tap; Amina laughs. Music begins – soft piano.
SHOT 4: Text on screen: "£25 can bring clean water to a child for life."
VOICE-OVER: "Amina's walk can end today." Logo and website.

Explain how the storyboard creates an emotional journey for the viewer.
items.answer: Camera shots move from close-up on tired feet (hardship, empathy) to a wide shot showing the long distance, then a close-up of the laughing face. Sound changes from wind and silence (emptiness) to piano music when the tap appears, signalling hope. Captions give the facts and the donation request.
items.markingKey: Camera shots move from close-up on tired feet (hardship, empathy) to a wide shot showing the long distance, then a close-up of the laughing face. Sound changes from wind and silence (emptiness) to piano music when the tap appears, signalling hope. Captions give the facts and the donation request. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Describe two camera shots you would use in a 20-second video advert for a reusable bottle and explain why.
items.answer: Any two valid shots with reasons, e.g. a close-up of plastic bottles in the sea (shock), a wide shot of a clean beach with a person drinking from the bottle (solution).
items.markingKey: Any two valid shots with reasons, e.g. a close-up of plastic bottles in the sea (shock), a wide shot of a clean beach with a person drinking from the bottle (solution).

items.stem:
Read the following campaign poster from a youth environmental group.

[Image: a mountain of discarded clothes in a desert; a single price tag in the foreground reads "€4.99".]
WORN ONCE. THROWN AWAY. STILL HERE IN 200 YEARS.
The world buys about 80 billion new garments a year.
Before you buy, ask: Do I need it? Will I wear it 30 times?
#ThinkBeforeYouThread  –  Fashion Forward Youth Network

How does the poster challenge young people's attitudes to buying clothes?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The image juxtaposes a tiny €4.99 price tag with a mountain of waste, revealing hidden costs. The tricolon traces a garment's short use and long afterlife, and the statistic shows global scale. Rhetorical questions give a personal test, and the punning hashtag makes the campaign memorable and shareable.

The tricolon traces a garment's short use and long afterlife, and the statistic shows global scale. Rhetorical questions give a personal test, and the punning hashtag makes the campaign memorable and shareable. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem:
Read the following infographic from a health website for teenagers.

[Headline in large white letters on dark blue: ARE YOU RUNNING ON EMPTY?]
[Icon of a phone battery at 20%: Teenagers need 8–10 hours of sleep a night.]
[Bar chart: 7 in 10 teenagers get less than 8 hours on school nights.]
[Three icons in a row: a moon, a closed book, a phone with a cross through it – "Same bedtime. Wind down. Screens off 1 hour before bed."]
[Small print: Source: national adolescent health survey, 2023.]

Discuss how the words and the image work together in this text.
items.answer: The low phone-battery icon is a symbol teenagers instantly recognise, linking tiredness to something from their daily lives; the dark blue background suggests night, and three simple icons make the advice quick to remember.
items.markingKey: The low phone-battery icon is a symbol teenagers instantly recognise, linking tiredness to something from their daily lives; the dark blue background suggests night, and three simple icons make the advice quick to remember. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "formal register"?
options: An opposing point that a writer acknowledges and then answers (rebuts)
A question asked for effect, not for an answer, to make the audience think
Language suited to official or serious situations, avoiding slang and contractions
A formal letter written to convince a specific reader to take action or change their view
items.answer: Language suited to official or serious situations, avoiding slang and contractions
items.markingKey: C. "formal register" is language suited to official or serious situations, avoiding slang and contractions.

items.stem: Explain why leaflets use bullet points and headings.
items.answer: They make information easy to scan quickly, so busy readers can find the key points.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They make information easy to scan quickly, so busy readers can find the key points. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Hana writes: "Persuasive writing should only include your own opinion." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Effective persuasion supports opinions with evidence, examples and statistics and addresses counterarguments.
items.markingKey: Effective persuasion supports opinions with evidence, examples and statistics and addresses counterarguments. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following leaflet from a school eco-club in Singapore.

GO PLASTIC-FREE THIS JULY!
Did you know? Our canteen throws away about 900 plastic cups every week. That's over 30,000 a year – enough to reach the top of Marina Bay Sands if you stacked them!
What can YOU do?
• Bring a reusable bottle (free refills at the new water fountains).
• Say "no straw, please".
• Join our Thursday lunchtime clean-up.
Small changes. Big difference. Sign up at the eco-club table by Friday!

Rewrite the leaflet's message as a 60-second assembly speech to Grade 8 students.
items.answer: Indicative content: a hook (question or statistic), spoken features (direct address, repetition), two or three actions, a clear call to action; register suited to peers.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: a hook (question or statistic), spoken features (direct address, repetition), two or three actions, a clear call to action; register suited to peers. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "A polite letter is more persuasive than an angry one."
items.answer: A firm but polite tone is usually more persuasive, because it keeps the reader listening while still showing that the issue matters.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: politeness builds respect and trust; angry letters can be dismissed. Arguments against: strong feelings can show urgency; some issues require forceful language. Supported judgement: A firm but polite tone is usually more persuasive, because it keeps the reader listening while still showing that the issue matters.

items.stem: Write the opening paragraph of a persuasive letter to your local council asking for a pedestrian crossing outside your school.
items.answer: Formal salutation; clear statement of purpose; one piece of evidence or a reason; formal register. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: Formal salutation; clear statement of purpose; one piece of evidence or a reason; formal register. 1 mark each.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "rhetorical question"?
options: A list of three words, phrases or ideas that makes a point memorable
A group defined by characteristics such as age, gender, income or interests
A question asked for effect, not for an answer, to make the audience think
The specific group of people a text is aimed at
items.answer: A question asked for effect, not for an answer, to make the audience think
items.markingKey: C. "rhetorical question" is a question asked for effect, not for an answer, to make the audience think.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "What a text is trying to do: for example to persuade, inform, entertain, advise or explain"?
options: purpose
counterargument
call to action
rhetorical question
items.answer: purpose
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of purpose.

items.stem: Explain why video adverts use changes in sound and music.
items.answer: Sound shapes the viewer's feelings – silence can suggest emptiness or hardship, while music can signal hope – guiding the emotional response.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a persuasive letter and a leaflet.
items.answer: A persuasive letter addresses one specific reader in continuous formal paragraphs; a leaflet addresses a wider audience using headings, bullet points and images for quick reading.
items.markingKey: A persuasive letter addresses one specific reader in continuous formal paragraphs; a leaflet addresses a wider audience using headings, bullet points and images for quick reading. items.stem: Explain why statistics make persuasive texts more convincing.
items.answer: Numbers seem objective and factual, so they make claims appear proven and reliable (logos).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Numbers seem objective and factual, so they make claims appear proven and reliable (logos). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following letter from a student to her local council in Manchester.

Dear Councillor Patel,
I am writing to ask you to reconsider the decision to close Levenshulme Library.
For many students in my area, the library is the only quiet place to study. My flat has five people and one table. The library has Wi-Fi, printers and Mrs Okafor, who has helped me with every homework project since I was eight.
Closing it would save money this year, but it would cost our community far more in the future.
I would be grateful if you could meet our youth group to discuss alternatives.
Yours sincerely,
Amira Hassan (age 14)

Which features of this text could you borrow for your own persuasive writing? Explain two.
items.answer: It is a letter. Conventions: an address or salutation, a clear purpose in the opening, paragraphs that develop the case and a sign-off. In this text, for example: "My flat has five people and one table." (personal anecdote) and stating the purpose in the first sentence, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.

options: "Amina's walk can end today."
"The well is 6 km away."
"Visit our website."
"Our logo is blue."
items.answer: "Amina's walk can end today."
items.markingKey: A. It appeals to the viewer's feelings about a named child.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "demographic"?
options: A group defined by characteristics such as age, gender, income or interests
A formal letter written to convince a specific reader to take action or change their view
A camera shot that shows a face or object in detail, often to create emotion
Words chosen to make the audience feel strong emotions such as pity, guilt or anger
items.answer: A group defined by characteristics such as age, gender, income or interests
items.markingKey: A. "demographic" is a group defined by characteristics such as age, gender, income or interests.

items.stem: Explain why images are often more important than words in advertisements.
items.answer: Images are processed instantly and create emotion and associations (connotations) that words alone cannot, so they grab attention quickly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Images are processed instantly and create emotion and associations (connotations) that words alone cannot, so they grab attention quickly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Persuasive writing should only include your own opinion." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Effective persuasion supports opinions with evidence, examples and statistics and addresses counterarguments.
items.markingKey: Effective persuasion supports opinions with evidence, examples and statistics and addresses counterarguments. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between emotive language and statistics.
items.answer: Emotive language persuades through feelings (pathos); statistics persuade through apparent facts and logic (logos). Strong persuasion often combines both.
items.markingKey: Emotive language persuades through feelings (pathos); statistics persuade through apparent facts and logic (logos). Strong persuasion often combines both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why advertisers must identify their target audience before writing.
items.answer: Language, images and placement must appeal to the specific interests, values and age of the audience to persuade them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Language, images and placement must appeal to the specific interests, values and age of the audience to persuade them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a print advertisement and a video advertisement.
items.answer: A print advert relies on a single image, layout and text that readers can study; a video advert uses moving images, camera shots, sound, music and time to tell a mini-story.
items.markingKey: A print advert relies on a single image, layout and text that readers can study; a video advert uses moving images, camera shots, sound, music and time to tell a mini-story. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following persuasive letter from a student to her head teacher in Copenhagen.

Dear Ms Larsen,
I am writing on behalf of the Grade 8 class to propose a covered bike shelter for our school.
At present, 140 students cycle to school, but there are only 40 spaces. Bikes are left in the rain and two were stolen last month.
A shelter would keep bikes safe, encourage more students to cycle, and support our city's aim to be carbon-neutral by 2025.
Surely a school that teaches us about climate change should make the green choice the easy choice?
Yours sincerely,
Freja Nielsen, Grade 8B

Which features of this text could you borrow for your own persuasive writing? Explain two.
items.answer: It is a letter. Conventions: an address or salutation, a clear purpose in the opening, paragraphs that develop the case and a sign-off. In this text, for example: "keep bikes safe, encourage more students to cycle, and support our city's aim" (tricolon) and problem – solution – benefits – challenge, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.
items.markingKey: It is a letter. Conventions: an address or salutation, a clear purpose in the opening, paragraphs that develop the case and a sign-off. In this text, for example: "keep bikes safe, encourage more students to cycle, and support our city's aim" (tricolon) and problem – solution – benefits – challenge, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: A student claims: "Statistics in adverts are always true and complete." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Statistics can be selected, rounded or presented without context; readers should check sources.
items.markingKey: Statistics can be selected, rounded or presented without context; readers should check sources. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a 14-year-old to a regional youth climate conference in Fiji.

Bula, everyone. My name is Losana, and my island is disappearing.
Not in a hundred years. Now. Last year, the sea came into my grandmother's kitchen. Twice.
Some people say: you are just a child, what can you do? I say: I am a child, and that is exactly why I am here. Because it is my future you are spending.
So I ask you three things: listen to islands, cut emissions, and fund the walls that keep the sea out of kitchens.
Vinaka vakalevu – thank you.

Identify the intended audience of this speech. Support your answer with one reference to the text.
items.answer: Delegates at a youth climate conference, including adults with power to act; she addresses them directly ("it is my future you are spending"). Supporting evidence: "Not in a hundred years. Now." (short sentences) – the short sentences correct the audience's assumption and stress urgency.
items.markingKey: Delegates at a youth climate conference, including adults with power to act; she addresses them directly ("it is my future you are spending"). Supporting evidence: "Not in a hundred years. Now." (short sentences) – the short sentences correct the audience's assumption and stress urgency. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following storyboard description of a 30-second charity video advertisement.

SHOT 1 (close-up): A girl's feet in torn sandals walk along a dry riverbed. Sound: wind, no music.
SHOT 2 (wide shot): She carries a yellow jerrycan towards a distant well. Caption: "Amina walks 6 km for water. Every day."
SHOT 3 (close-up): Water pours from a new tap; Amina laughs. Music begins – soft piano.
SHOT 4: Text on screen: "£25 can bring clean water to a child for life."
VOICE-OVER: "Amina's walk can end today." Logo and website.

Analyse how camera shots and sound are used to persuade viewers in this video advertisement.
items.answer: Camera shots move from close-up on tired feet (hardship, empathy) to a wide shot showing the long distance, then a close-up of the laughing face. Sound changes from wind and silence (emptiness) to piano music when the tap appears, signalling hope. Captions give the facts and the donation request.
items.markingKey: Camera shots move from close-up on tired feet (hardship, empathy) to a wide shot showing the long distance, then a close-up of the laughing face. Sound changes from wind and silence (emptiness) to piano music when the tap appears, signalling hope. Captions give the facts and the donation request. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: A student claims: "Persuasive writing should only include your own opinion." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Effective persuasion supports opinions with evidence, examples and statistics and addresses counterarguments.
items.markingKey: Effective persuasion supports opinions with evidence, examples and statistics and addresses counterarguments. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column by a Year 10 student in a school magazine in Melbourne.

Why I've Changed My Mind About Uniforms
In Year 7 I thought school uniform was a prison sentence in polyester. I wanted to wear my own clothes, my own style, my own identity.
Then I met Jonah. Jonah's family couldn't afford the brands everyone else wore. On mufti days he 'forgot' and wore his blazer anyway.
A uniform doesn't erase who we are. It erases the price tag.
Yes, the jumpers are itchy. Yes, the colour is a crime against fashion. But I'd rather be itchy than watch a friend hide.

Answer the following question in a well-organised response of about 250 words: How does the writer persuade readers to change their minds about school uniform?
items.answer: The writer first agrees with the reader ("a prison sentence in polyester"), building trust through humour. The anecdote about Jonah and the scare quotes around "forgot" create sympathy and reveal hidden inequality. The antithesis "It doesn't erase who we are. It erases the price tag" reframes the debate, and the concessions ("Yes, the jumpers are itchy") make the writer seem fair before the emotional final line.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The writer first agrees with the reader ("a prison sentence in polyester"), building trust through humour. The anecdote about Jonah and the scare quotes around "forgot" create sympathy and reveal hidden inequality. The antithesis "It doesn't erase who we are. It erases the price tag" reframes the debate, and the concessions ("Yes, the jumpers are itchy") make the writer seem fair before the emotional final line. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Advertisers aimed at teenagers are more manipulative than those aimed at adults."
items.answer: All advertising seeks to influence; teenagers may be especially targeted through social media, so media literacy matters for every audience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: teenagers are influenced by peer pressure and social media; adverts use insecurities about image. Arguments against: adult adverts also exploit fears (health, status); many teenagers are media-literate and critical. Supported judgement: All advertising seeks to influence; teenagers may be especially targeted through social media, so media literacy matters for every audience. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem:
Read the following campaign poster from a youth environmental group.

[Image: a mountain of discarded clothes in a desert; a single price tag in the foreground reads "€4.99".]
WORN ONCE. THROWN AWAY. STILL HERE IN 200 YEARS.
The world buys about 80 billion new garments a year.
Before you buy, ask: Do I need it? Will I wear it 30 times?
#ThinkBeforeYouThread  –  Fashion Forward Youth Network

Answer the following question in a well-organised response of about 250 words: How does the poster challenge young people's attitudes to buying clothes?
items.answer: The image juxtaposes a tiny €4.99 price tag with a mountain of waste, revealing hidden costs. The tricolon traces a garment's short use and long afterlife, and the statistic shows global scale. Rhetorical questions give a personal test, and the punning hashtag makes the campaign memorable and shareable.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The image juxtaposes a tiny €4.99 price tag with a mountain of waste, revealing hidden costs. The tricolon traces a garment's short use and long afterlife, and the statistic shows global scale. Rhetorical questions give a personal test, and the punning hashtag makes the campaign memorable and shareable. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.
